title: The thermal stability of nanobainitic microstructure and its effect on the mechanical properties of a high-carbon steel manufactured by the thermomechanical treatment
abstract: Abstract The present study investigates the effect of tempering on the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a nanostructured bainitic steel produced through a novel thermomechanical treatment. In this study, tempering was applied to separately prepared specimens to reproduce the thermal exposure associated with the anticipated service conditions of the steel, rather than as part of its conventional heat-treatment route. Tempering was carried out at temperatures ranging from 150 °C to 600°C for 2 h to evaluate the stability and transformation behavior of the nanobainitic microstructure. A combination of synchrotron X-ray diffraction, dilatometric analysis, scanning electron microscopy observation, and mechanical testing was employed to investigate the structural changes and their influence on strength and ductility. At lower tempering temperatures (150–360 °C and 450 °C), microstructural changes were primarily determined by carbon diffusion within the bainitic ferrite and retained austenite. This led to a decrease in the volume fraction of the retained austenite and an increase in the volume fraction of the bainitic ferrite. Additionally, these temperatures promoted the precipitation of ε-carbides and cementite, as well as bainitic transformation during tempering and martensitic transformation during cooling. At elevated temperatures (500–600 °C), the decomposition of retained austenite into ferrite and cementite, indicating further carbon redistribution and phase transformation. The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS) of tempered specimens were lower than those of the untempered condition. However, a substantial increase in YS was observed at 450 °C, surpassing the untempered value by 131 MPa. This phenomenon is presumably attributable to the impeding of dislocation motion by interfacial cementite precipitation.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The main disadvantage of nanostructured bainitic steel is the long duration of the isothermal heat treatment, which is essential for obtaining the nanobainitic microstructure. This treatment must be carried out at a very low temperature, depending on the chemical composition of the tested steel, but above the martensite start temperature (M S ) in order to avoid martensitic transformation [ 7 ]. In the case of high-carbon, low-alloyed nanobainitic steels, the conventional heat treatment is usually performed at 200°C for 9 or even 10 days [ 8 ,  9 ]. As is well known, completing the nanobainitic transformation at a given temperature requires exceeding the carbon concentration in retained austenite, as determined by the T₀ and T₀′ lines, introduced in the thermodynamic model by Bhadeshia et al. [ 10 ,  11 ]. Recent studies have focused on the reduction of the incubation time required for retained austenite to reach the necessary carbon concentration by increasing the overall thermodynamic driving force for the bainitic transformation [ 12 ]. This objective has been accomplished through a variety of methodologies, including the refinement of the initial austenite grain size [ 13 ], addition of Co and Al to the steel’s chemical composition [ 9 ] and introduction of pre-formed martensite [ 14 ]. Other strategies include the application of stress or prior deformation [ 15 ] after austenitization and before the nanobainitic transformation, as well as the implementation of a two-step austempering treatment [ 16 ]. This overview should also include ausforming process in the temperature range below austenitization and above the bainitic transformation, which also significantly accelerates the kinetics of the bainitic transformation [ 17 ].

Among these methods, the most effective approach to accelerate the kinetics of the nanobainitic transformation has been found to be the application of external stress, either below or above the yield strength of the parent austenite, during the initial stage of the transformation. In this way, not only is the incubation time significantly reduced, but the mechanical properties of the steel remain at a high level. In a recent study, when stress below the yield strength of parent austenite was applied, the total time of the nanobainitic transformation was reduced to 30 min at 200°C, while maintaining excellent mechanical properties, including an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1862 MPa, yield strength (YS) of 1287 MPa, and elongation of 11.8% [ 18 ]. A similar effect was reported by Guo et al. [ 19 ] where isothermal heat treatment was conducted with an externally applied strain of 40% at a strain rate of 5 s⁻¹ and a temperature of 300 °C for 4 h. In that case, the resulting mechanical properties included a UTS of 1900 MPa, YS of 1500 MPa, and an elongation of 24.4%.

Although nanostructured bainitic steel produced with external stress or strain during isothermal treatment has excellent mechanical properties and a significantly reduced transformation time, its industrial application may still be limited. One primary constraint is the difficulty of integrating these steels into conventional industrial processes, like welding techniques [ 20 ]. These post-processing operations involve unavoidable thermal exposure, and it has been reported that nanobainitic microstructures decompose into ferrite and carbides at elevated temperatures [ 21 ]. Additionally, Peet et al. [ 22 ] and Santajuana et al. [ 23 ] demonstrated that the nanobainitic steel produced via conventional heat treatment cannot withstand prolonged exposure to temperatures above 500°C. Nevertheless, post-treatment processes are often employed to achieve an optimal balance of strength, hardness, ductility, and toughness, while simultaneously relieving residual stresses. Therefore, improving the thermal stability of nanobainitic steels is crucial for their wider industrial use, especially for nanostructured bainitic grades. Although the decomposition behavior of carbide-free nanobainitic steel obtained via conventional heat treatment is relatively well investigated, the variant produced through thermomechanical heat treatment (with additional external stress) is still in the early stages of microstructural and mechanical characterization, with limited understanding of the underlying bainitic nucleation mechanisms [ 15 ]. Furthermore, nanobainitic microstructures that form during isothermal transformation with external stress or strain tend to retain significant amounts of austenite, primarily in a blocky morphology [ 18 ,  19 ,  24 ]. In such cases, the thermal stability and decomposition mechanisms of retained austenite are critical factors that influence the steel’s performance and long-term applicability.

Thus, this study primarily aims to investigate the decomposition behavior of retained austenite and the evolution of microstructural constituents parameters during indirect thermal exposure (i.e., heating followed by cooling [ 25 ]) in high-carbon nanobainitic steel produced by a novel controlled thermomechanical heat treatment process. This research focuses on the detailed microstructural evolution, phase transformation behavior, and associated mechanical properties of nanostructured bainitic steel tempered at temperatures ranging from 150°C to 600°C for 2 h. The objective is to provide theoretical insights and practical guidance for the further development and industrial implementation of nanostructured bainitic steels.

sections.heading: Experimental procedures
paragraphs: The chemical composition of the supplied high-carbon nanobainitic steel was as follows (in wt%): Fe-0.78 C-1.67Si-2.45Mn-1.35Cr-0.21Mo-1.30Al. The investigated material was initially obtained in the form of a cast ingot with a diameter of approximately 300 mm and subsequently subjected to thermomechanical processing to obtain the nanobainitic microstructure. This process included homogenization at 1250°C, followed by six hot-rolling passes performed in the austenitic temperature range. During rolling, the ingot diameter was reduced from approximately 300 mm to 80 mm, while the rolling temperature decreased from 1250°C to a minimum finishing temperature of 950°C. Then, it was rapidly cooled to the bainitic transformation range using pressurized water. The cooling conditions were selected to provide an average cooling rate of approximately 1 °C/s, sufficient to suppress pearlitic transformation and promote bainitic transformation. Finally, isothermal heat treatment was applied. During isothermal treatment, additional stress was applied at 200°C for 10 s under stress below the yield strength of the parent austenite (250 MPa). Afterwards, the steel was cooled to 190 °C and held for 30 min to achieve full bainitic transformation. More detailed information on the thermo-mechanical processing route can be found in [ 18 ]. To evaluate the thermal stability of the retained austenite in the obtained nanobainitic microstructure, a tempering process was conducted using a Bahr 805D high-resolution dilatometer. Cylindrical samples measuring 4 mm in diameter and 10 mm in length were tested in an argon atmosphere. Quartz pushrods measured the relative change in length (RCL), and a type K thermocouple controlled the temperature. The steel was held at various temperatures ranging from 150°C to 600°C for 2 h during tempering. In order to analyze the thermal effects in detail, the RCL was recorded as a function of temperature during continuous heating, cooling and tempering. For continuous heating and cooling, the first derivative of the RCL (DRCL) was calculated to determine possibility phase transformations temperatures.

Further microstructural observations were performed using a FEI SEM XL30 scanning electron microscope equipped with an EDAX GEMINI 4000 energy-dispersive X-ray spectrometer. The samples were polished and etched in Nital (2% HNO₃ and 98% CH₃OH) at room temperature to reveal the transformed microstructures. Hardness measurements were carried out using the Vickers method (HV5) on a Zwick/ZHU 250 machine with a 49 N load applied for 15 s. Tensile tests after tempering at the selected temperatures were performed using a Shimadzu Autograph AG-X Plus testing machine operated at a strain rate of 10 − 3  s − 1 . Strain was measured using a TRViewX video extensometer system. The geometry of the tensile specimen, together with its dimensions, is presented in Fig.  1 .

sections.heading: Initial microstructure
Effect of tempering on the dilatometry behavior
paragraphs: Fig. 2 a  Relative change in length (RCL) and  b  first derivative of RCL (DRCL) during continuous heating of the tested steel up to the austenitization temperature; nbm denotes the nanobainitic microstructure

Figure  3  shows the dilatometry curves illustrating the RCL as a function of tempering time during the heating and cooling of the tested steel within the tempering temperature range of 150–360°C. Positive dilatometric effects of 0.01% and 0.14% were observed at tempering temperatures of 150°C and 210°C, respectively, indicating the occurrence of bainitic transformation from retained austenite at these temperatures [ 28 ]. Notably, the amount of newly formed bainite is expected to increase with increasing tempering temperature. However, for the sample tempered at 290°C, the RCL remains nearly constant, as shown in Fig.  3 c. This suggests an absence of further transformation. In contrast, contraction of − 0.01% is observed at 360°C (Fig.  3 d), which can be attributed to the relaxation of compressive stresses induced during quenching or the precipitation of cementite from transition carbides. Figure  4  shows the RCL as a function of temperature within the tempering range of 450–600°C, as well as the RCL versus tempering time. Contraction is consistently observed within this temperature range. At 450°C, contraction reaches − 0.06% after 2 h of tempering and changes as the temperature increases. At 500°C and 600°C, the contraction values are − 0.09% and − 0.04%, respectively. Contraction ceases after approximately 3500 s and 200 s, respectively. This contraction is directly associated with the precipitation of cementite. The precipitation concurrently reduces the stability of both retained austenite and supersaturated bainitic ferrite, leading to their decomposition into a mixture of ferrite and cementite. This is evidenced by the subsequent positive change in RCL during tempering [ 26 ]. At 500°C, this decomposition begins after 3500 s and continues until the end of the tempering cycle. At 600°C, decomposition begins as early as 200 s and is complete by approximately 3200 s, as indicated by the plateau in the RCL curve. An inflection in the RCL versus temperature curve is observed during cooling in the 450–600°C tempering range (Fig.  4 a-c). This inflection is attributed to the martensitic transformation of retained austenite depleted of carbon due to cementite precipitation [ 25 ]. The martensite start temperatures (M S ) identified were 146°C, 240°C, and 320°C for tempering treatments at 450°C, 500°C, and 600°C, respectively. These results imply the existence of martensite in the final microstructure after tempering at these temperatures. Similar behavior during the tempering of nanobainitic microstructures was reported by Wang et al. [ 29 ] for high-carbon steel produced via conventional heat treatment at 210 °C for 72 h.

sections.heading: Effect of tempering of the mechanical properties
paragraphs: Tempering nanostructured bainitic steel substantially alters its mechanical behavior, which is directly associated with underlying microstructural transformations. As illustrated in Fig.  8 a and b, tempering affects the material’s stress–strain response and hardness. The mechanical response at 500°C is characterized by a rapid loss of ductility and a sudden fracture shortly beyond the yield point, indicating that the material is unable to sustain significant plastic deformation under these conditions. Conversely, samples tempered within the 150–450°C and 600°C ranges exhibited ductile fracture behavior characterized by plastic flow beyond the ultimate tensile strength (UTS). In terms of hardness, tempering generally resulted in a reduction compared to the as-transformed condition. Within the 150–450°C range, hardness remained relatively stable, fluctuating slightly around 560 HV5 (e.g., 556 HV5 at 150°C and 558 HV5 at 450°C). Tempering at 500°C led to an increase in hardness to 579 HV5, which can be attributed to the formation of fresh martensite resulting from the transformation of retained austenite during cooling [ 35 ]. A sharp decline in hardness was observed at 600°C, dropping to 472 HV5. This reduction is linked to the complete decomposition of the nanobainitic microstructure, which leads to the formation of a softer phase mixture.
Fig. 8 a  Representative stress–strain curves and  b  variation of hardness values for the nanostructured bainitic tested steel after tempering at various temperatures

Figure  9  illustrates the evolution of the strength (Fig.  9 a) and elongation (Fig.  9 b) values of nanostructured bainitic steel as a function of tempering temperature. Untempered steel exhibited an ultimate tensile strength (UTS) of 1703 MPa, a yield strength (YS) of 1190 MPa, and an elongation of 8.9%. These values differ slightly from those reported in the previous study [ 18 ], which can be attributed to differences in the geometry of the specimens used in the current work. Compared to the untempered condition, a general decrease in UTS was observed with tempering. In the temperature range of 150°C to 450°C, the UTS values were 1516 MPa, 1554 MPa, 1502 MPa, 1541 MPa, and 1542 MPa for tempering at 150°C, 210°C, 290°C, 360°C, and 450°C, respectively. Beyond 450°C, a more pronounced decline was noted, with UTS values decreasing to 1375 MPa at 500°C and 1240 MPa at 600°C. A similar trend was observed for the yield strength (YS) values. In most cases, YS was lower than that of the untempered steel, except for tempering at 450°C and 600°C. Specifically, the YS reached 1016 MPa, 1087 MPa, 1084 MPa, and 1035 MPa at 150°C, 210°C, 290°C, and 360°C, respectively. At 450°C, YS increased by approximately 185 MPa, reaching 1375 MPa. This strengthening effect is likely related to the precipitation of cementite and the transformation of ε-carbides [ 36 ], as confirmed by synchrotron X-ray diffraction analysis (Fig.  5 ). Following this, YS decreased significantly to 696 MPa at 500°C and increased again to 977 MPa at 600°C. Elongation exhibited a complex response to tempering. At 150°C, elongation increased by approximately 2.9% relative to the untempered condition, reaching 12.8%. It then decreased to 9.8% at 210°C, followed by an increase to 11.1% at 290°C. In this temperature range (150–290°C), elongation remained higher than in the untempered state. At 360°C, elongation nearly returned to the initial level of 8.8%. However, elongation decreased significantly at 450°C and 500°C, dropping to 5.8% and 1.8%, respectively. Consistent with the trend observed in YS, elongation increased again at 600°C, reaching 5.7%.
Fig. 9 a  Evolution of ultimate tensile strength (UTS) and yield strength (YS), and  b  elongation, as a function of increasing tempering temperature for the nanostructured bainitic tested steel

sections.heading: Evolution of the nanobainitic microstructure with tempering temperature
paragraphs: The fourth stage occurs at 600°C and involves the complete decomposition of retained austenite into ferrite and cementite. Additionally, ε-carbides were no longer detectable in the synchrotron X-ray diffraction patterns (Fig.  5 ), indicating their complete transformation into cementite at this temperature. At this temperature, the diffusivity of carbon within all microstructural constituents is significantly high, which promotes intensified cementite precipitation. Consequently, the carbon concentration in ferrite approaches its equilibrium value. Thus, the microstructure at this stage consists of two equilibrium phases: ferrite and cementite. Complete decomposition of the microstructure was confirmed by dilatometric analysis (Fig.  4 c). The relative change in length (RCL) curve reached a plateau after approximately 200 s of tempering at 600°C, indicating cessation of diffusion transformation. In addition, trace amounts of martensite may be noticeable.

Based on the above discussion, the microstructural evolution of the tested nanobainitic steel produced via a novel thermomechanical treatment in the temperature range of 150–600°C is summarized in Fig.  10 .

Fig. 10 Scheme of nanobainitic microstructure decomposition of nanostructured bainite steel manufactured by the novel thermomechanical treatment during the tempering treatment at temperatures ranging from 150°C to 600°C for 2 h

In the present study, it is important to note that cementite precipitation is suppressed during tempering due to the presence of specific alloying elements in the steel’s chemical composition. Elements such as Mn, Cr, and Mo delay cementite precipitation as the tempering temperature increases due to their high solubility in ferrite and austenite. Consequently, the rate of carbon diffusion decreases, delaying the transition from ε-carbide to cementite [ 50 ,  51 ]. Additionally, silicon (Si) inhibits carbide growth and retards martensite decomposition during tempering. Elements such as molybdenum (Mo) and chromium (Cr) may also remain partially dissolved in ferrite following martensite decomposition during cooling, which further slows down diffusional processes [ 52 ,  53 ].

sections.heading: Relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties
paragraphs: Following the tensile and hardness tests, significant differences in the mechanical properties were observed for the nanostructured bainitic steel subjected to tempering in the temperature range of 150–600°C. A slight decrease in ultimate tensile strength (UTS) was recorded for specimens tempered between 150°C and 450°C. Then, there was a substantial drop in UTS for specimens tempered at 500°C and 600°C. These changes were attributed to several concurrent microstructural phenomena. The nanobainitic steel’s high initial strength was due to a combination of carbon-induced solid solution strengthening, dislocation strengthening, and bainitic ferrite grain refinement [ 38 ]. During tempering, carbon redistribution within the microstructural constituents was activated, resulting in the formation of ε-carbides at 150–360°C and cementite (θ) precipitation at 450–600°C [ 29 ,  54 ] These precipitations reduced the carbon concentration in bainitic ferrite (Fig.  6 ), thereby weakening the solid solution strengthening mechanism. Simultaneously, the metastable bainitic structure gradually recovered toward a thermodynamic equilibrium state [ 26 ], as shown in Fig.  11 , which was reflected by a decrease in dislocation density. Furthermore, the formation of newly formed bainite promoted bainitic ferrite coarsening with increasing tempering temperature [ 29 ], contributing to the observed decline in UTS. At higher tempering temperatures (450–600°C), the retained austenite decomposed into ferrite and cementite. Additionally, due to carbon depletion, the retained austenite transformed into martensite during cooling after tempering [ 55 ]. These effects caused further deterioration in UTS. An increase in hardness (Fig.  8 b) and brittle fracture behavior (Fig.  8 a) was observed at 500°C. This was attributed to the formation of cementite and the transformation of retained austenite into martensite during cooling [ 26 ,  56 ]. While this response may resemble secondary hardening, it should be noted that secondary hardening does not occur in nanostructured bainitic steels [ 57 ].

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Tempering of the nanobainitic steel produced by a novel thermomechanical treatment was carried out at temperatures ranging from 150°C to 600°C. In order to investigate the stability and evolution of the nanobainitic microstructure, detailed structural, dilatometric, and diffraction analyses were conducted.
